records.our_prose: The desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) grow grape tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar built around a hard summer heat exclusion. The main crop is transplanted in the mild winter window, December through mid-March, and harvested from spring into June; then June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs past 95°F and often above 110°F, which collapses viable pollen), so planting pauses. A second, fall crop is set out in September as the heat breaks and produces through the mild desert winter into January. This summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance: unlike the milder southeastern Gulf summer, desert peak heat stops fruit set even for heat-tolerant grape types. Confirm local frost and heat timing, which vary across the desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

records.our_prose: The North Coast (Monterey County north, including the cool marine-influenced counties such as Marin) grows grape tomatoes as a single short warm season set by heat availability rather than frost. Transplants go out in May, later than the interior valleys, because coastal summers are cool and nights can sit below 55°F in any month. A single planting then carries one harvest through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten, ahead of the late coastal first frost. This is the cool-limited case: the limiting factor is insufficient summer heat, not a midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cool-summer-adapted varieties and the warmest, most sheltered sites do best, and microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm local conditions. records.our_prose: The Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11, south of about Orlando) grows grape tomatoes on a single long cool-season window rather than the spring-and-fall pattern of cooler regions. Because frost is rare, the planting window runs continuously from the fall transplant in September and October through February, the last month UF/IFAS lists for planting tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Production carries through the mild winter and spring. The limiting season is summer: in July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) cause blossom drop and fruit-set failure. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; grape types are heat resistant, so the exclusion narrows to those two peak months for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Start seed indoors in August for fall transplanting, and choose fast-maturing grape types. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

records.our_prose: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows grape tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Transplants go out a week or two after the last spring frost, once nights stay above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through summer until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: unlike the Southeast or the desert valleys, northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the winter gaps are frost pauses and the season is uninterrupted between them. Grape types (65 to 75 days from transplant) are well suited to short seasons and ripen before first frost even in zone 3. The cold end (zones 3 and 4) leans on fast-maturing varieties and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters), while the warm end (zones 6 and 7) has room for a second transplanting in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

records.our_prose: Rotate nightshades to a fresh bed every 3 years minimum. Soilborne pathogens, particularly Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici), Verticillium wilt, and early blight (Alternaria solani), can persist in soil or on plant debris for multiple seasons. records.our_prose: Stop high-nitrogen feeding when flowers appear and switch to a high-potassium, low-nitrogen feed. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth by stimulating cell division and chlorophyll synthesis, exactly what you want early in the season and exactly what you don't want once flowering starts; potassium plays a different role: it regulates stomatal opening, drives sugar transport from leaves into developing fruit, and is critical for cell wall formation in the fruit itself. A tomato-specific or high-K fertilizer (look for an NPK ratio with a high last number, such as 5-10-10 or 4-12-8) used from first flowering onward translates directly into heavier, better-flavored fruit.
